chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Abu al-Subbah who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who married a woman and found her to be qarna' (unable to conceive). He said: 'This one does not conceive, and her husband is unable to have intercourse with her, and he returns her to her family in a humiliated state without a dowry.' I said: 'But if he had consummated the marriage with her?' He said: 'If he knew of that before marrying her (meaning the inability to have intercourse), then he had intercourse with her, he has accepted her. And if he did not know except after he had intercourse with her, then if he wishes afterwards he may keep her, and if he wishes he may divorce her.'

key_terms.دَخَلَ بِهَا: He entered with her (consummated the marriage).
key_terms.صَاغِرَةً: In a humiliated or lowly state.
key_terms.قَرْنَاءَ: A female who is unable to conceive or is barren; also interpreted as one who cannot be penetrated.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a husband discovers his wife's infertility or inability to consummate the marriage after they have already had intercourse?
ai.summary: In al-Istibsar, Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling on 'qarna' (often interpreted as a congenital defect preventing conception or penetration), highlighting the juristic distinction between pre-marital knowledge and post-consummation discovery. If the husband knew beforehand, he may return her without a full dowry (mahr al-sighr); if he discovered it after, he must choose between retaining her with full rights or divorcing her, reflecting the Shia principle of fairness in marital contracts.
